toc.title: Why do you want to change your state?
The body is compelled to self-regulate
The urge to do something is a gold mine
Optimal conditions depend on your state

blocks.p: We all search for that sense of inner balance, don't we? When it comes to finding calm or managing stress, our breath can be the first thing we turn to, although many of us, maybe even you, are unaware of our breathing. You probably became aware of it now, as I'm talking about it.

You might have heard the advice "breathe in to energize, breathe out to relax," or followed a prescribed breathing method, like box breathing, a certain number of seconds in and out, balloon breathing, color breathing, and whatever else is out there. And that's fine.

But what if the most effective path to feeling settled and connecting with yourself in the present moment isn't about imposing a rhythm, but tuning into the one your body naturally holds? I want to convince you of two things. First, you'll shift your polyvagal state naturally and compassionately by connecting with the way your body already wants to breathe. Second, if you don't, you're fundamentally rejecting your body, its needs, and actual long-lasting self-regulation.
What follows comes from a live Q&A I held with students. The questions are theirs; the answers are mine.

Someone asked: "Correct me if I'm wrong, but the in breath stimulates the sympathetic and the out breath stimulates the parasympathetic? So in the simplest form, you breathe in for two and out for four, or in for three and out for six?"

I personally don't like prescribed breathing: the counting, in for two, out for four, or whatever. I don't care for that. I would much prefer people mindfully connect with their breath as it is. There is value to extending your exhale. I like that. But I personally don't recommend counting, or having it be for a certain amount of time. I'd rather people focus on comfort level than on time.

I met with someone right before this Q&A, and she was doing prescribed breathing. She was counting, and that's fine. But I told her, "Why don't you just extend your exhale, but don't count. Just focus more on comfort." She tried it and said, "I liked that a lot more. I felt like I got more out of it. I was more focused. I was more mindful." Because otherwise you're counting, and I think that's counterintuitive to the mindfulness piece of it.

I know there's a lot of prescriptive breathing out there to relax, and sometimes to amp up: extending your inhale and decreasing your exhale. To me, that's very artificial. In one of my courses, I talk about something called induction: mobilizing by forcing yourself to mobilize. Prescribed breathing, with longer or more rapid inhales, would be one of those ways. But I don't like that stuff. I'd rather people connect with their natural state and their natural breath.

The only prescribed breathing I'll really give is maybe to mindfully take one deeper breath in, if the body wants to. You have to connect with what the body wants. Or mindfully extend the exhale. But not two seconds in, four seconds out. Not box breathing or color breathing. I'd rather we get out of our heads and connect more with what's happening bottom up.

blocks.h: Why do you want to change your state?

blocks.p: Someone else said: "I feel like I'm fairly in touch with my body and the present moment. But if I can change my state through induction, that's something I'm open to. I'd rather not wallow in my shutdown."

You said "in order to change my state." Why do you want to change your state? What's the point? Is it because I don't like it and I want to get rid of it? If that's the case, the way I think, and the way I teach, is that you're fundamentally rejecting the natural state of your body.

If you're doing that, I don't think natural self-regulation can occur. You can induce it. You can force some degree of shifting. But I don't think that's sustainable, and it's not a natural, mindful, compassionate connection with yourself.
What I would argue is that when we bring mindful connection to our breath from our safety state, it will change naturally, through self-regulation. Your body knows more than your brain does.

Our brain might say, "I don't like my state. I don't want to feel this way." And I don't blame anybody. It doesn't feel good to be in shutdown. So our conscious mind says, "I don't want to feel this way, so I'm going to change my breath, or drink an energy drink, or put some sort of time constraint on myself to induce mobility, to induce a state shift." That's our conscious plan. But the body is saying, "Just feel me. Pay attention to what I'm going through, and I'll take care of the rest. I can self-regulate."

That's really the shift I think needs to take place in how we think about these things. Path A, changing our breath and putting all these pressures on ourselves, is fundamentally rejecting the natural state of our body, which to me is the opposite of self-regulation. Path B, the one I'm laying out and try to teach, is to truly connect with the state of our body and see what happens. And what's going to happen is it's going to self-regulate. It has to. That's the natural compulsion of every living organism. I think our conscious mind gets in the way.

blocks.h: The body is compelled to self-regulate

blocks.p: Trauma means we're stuck in a defensive state. Not completely, not a hundred percent. Obviously it's more severe at times, but there's always some access to all these states at any given moment.

So even though we might be in a stuck defensive state, maybe stuck in shutdown, the body is still compelled to self-regulate. It's a homeostatic, biological thing. It has to self-regulate in order to function optimally. It wants to. It needs to. The more we can get out of the way consciously and allow that to happen, the better.

But we do things like scroll on our phone, and we distract it. We use drugs, we drink, we stay out late at night, we overeat, we undereat. And the body's like, "Just stop doing all that stuff so I can self-regulate."

The sooner we can cut out all that noise, the sooner the body can say, "Fricking finally. Thank you," and do what it needs to do. The problem is that it's very uncomfortable. It's not easy, and it requires a lot of safety activation. But once we can get those pieces in place, the self-regulation will happen. The coming out of defensive activation will happen.

blocks.h: The urge to do something is a gold mine

blocks.p: The same person said: "I tend to do better with productive ways of shifting state, like induction, versus the passive."

If it's true induction, where you're forcing it, I don't think it's sustainable, and it inherently rejects the fundamental need of our body. There's some degree of "I don't want this experience. I don't want to feel it. I don't want to connect with it. I'm tired of it."

And you said you do better with productive. That's totally fine. Nothing wrong with that at all. Love it. In my client work, my question would be: what does productive feel like? What's that urgency? What does it feel like? Instead of acting on it and doing something to feel differently, can we pause and feel that urgency, that pressure, that antsiness, whatever it is? That feeling of "I've got to do something" could be your body coming out of shutdown, with some sympathetic activation coming into the system.

So we want to feel that, mindfully. We want to connect with it, and then use it in a way that feels good for the body, rather than doing something to feel differently. That feeling of "I've got to do something" is a gold mine. There's a lot there to connect with if you mindfully, patiently feel into it. Where does it live in the body?

If you can feel that rising activation, we'll call it mobilization energy, it may not tell you to change your breath. It may tell you to pull, or push, or squeeze, or run, or sprint, or do squats. It may say, "No, we need to move. Let's use our muscles." Instead of breathing differently, or distracting ourselves with some project, your body might say, "This is what we need. Please do this so we can release all this activation that's coming up within us." But we won't know that until we stop rejecting how we feel and deeply feel how we feel. Then the body will tell us what it needs.

blocks.h: Optimal conditions depend on your state

blocks.p: Someone asked: "Can you discuss how to create the optimal conditions for the body to self-regulate?"

I want to separate something out first. What I'm not talking about is how to force ourselves to feel better. The optimal conditions for self-regulation depend on what state you're in. That's why you have to really connect with the state you're in.

If I'm in shutdown, typically people in shutdown want lower stimulation: quiet, lights usually down, or maybe natural lighting, sunlight. Lower stimulation in general. Then there are things specific to each of us. I like the scent of coconut. It does something for my body. It brings me to life. It's exciting. The next person might say, "That doesn't speak to me at all." So there are general conditions, like lower stimulation for shutdown, and more specific things for each of us as individuals. We have to listen to what our body needs.

If we can create that around us, it sets up the external conditions that help us get closer to feeling what it's like to be in shutdown, without forcing it or trying to change it. It's just listening to what I need, giving it to myself, and then looking back inward: how do I feel now? What's happening now?

Someone in flight or fight probably won't want lower stimulation. They want more stimulation. Instead of a closed, cozy space, they'll probably want more space: natural sunlight, being outside, green, pathways to walk down, space to run, space to walk. They don't want a closed room with the lights turned down. That doesn't speak to their system. So to create what they need, they would listen to their body and then give it what it needs.
When people I meet with say, "I wake up every morning and I feel anxious," I ask, "What do you do with that anxiety?"
They say, "I listen to a meditation to try to slow down, or I'll drink some tea."
And I'm like, "But that's not what your body wants. Your body wants movement. You wake up ready to move. Why are you doing the opposite?"
"Because I'm supposed to feel better. I'm supposed to feel safe. I'm supposed to feel calm."
"Okay, but you don't feel that way." So instead of giving yourself the opposite, what happens if the first thing you did when you got up was go for a walk?

I talked with someone last week who wakes up with a lot of anxiety, and we were brainstorming. I said, "What if you stood on your toes while you're making your eggs in the morning?" That way you're still flexing your muscles and giving your body a little more movement, and you can cook mindfully as well. Or what if you stood instead of sitting to eat your breakfast? What if you tensed and released your leg muscles while you eat? What if you listened to the needs of your body and used your anxiety, your energy, your mobilization, instead of ignoring it or trying to stuff it down to feel better?
Someone in the group said, "That seems counterintuitive. I would call that anti-logical. It's the opposite of what we typically do."

I fundamentally believe that the typical wisdom we bring to these things, maybe the cultural way of doing things, is wrong, and probably has a lot to do with why there are such rampant mental health problems. I really believe we are fundamentally doing things wrong. Instead, what if we just listened to what our body needs and provided it?

Try to trust the wisdom your body already has. Maybe I didn't convince you, and that's fine. But as you practice mindfulness and meditation, can you set aside the pressure to count, to measure, or to force your breathing to feel something other than what you're already feeling? Maybe now, or in some quiet moment, you can pause and simply ask: what does my body need right now?

The answer might not be what you expect. It might not be a longer exhale, but a gentle stretch, a moment of stillness, or a walk outside. Maybe it's a bigger breath. Maybe it's a breath into the belly, or into the chest. Just be as open as you can to whatever the answer is.
Remember, the goal isn't to fix. You're not broken. The goal is to connect and listen, and to allow your own system to guide you back to its natural state of safety and balance.
